title: The five-cord carriage
translation: Someone once told me that the carriage with five cords isn't kept for particular families. Whatever family you come from, once you reach the highest rank it can take you, you ride in one.
original: 「{車|くるま}の{五緒|いつつを}は{必|かなら}ず{人|ひと}によらず、ほどにつけて{極|きは}むる{官位|くわんゐ}に{至|いた}りぬれば{乗|の}るものなり。」とぞ、ある{人|ひと}おほせられし。
literal: 'The five-cord carriage does not necessarily depend on the person; when one has reached the office and rank that is the highest according to one's standing, one rides in it', someone said.

notes.text: An ox carriage with five decorative cords hanging from its blinds. Who could ride in which kind of carriage was fixed by rank, so a carriage showed everyone in the street who you were.
'Does not necessarily depend on the person', that is, on the family you were born into. Court families had a ceiling: each could rise only so high.

notes.quote: ほどにつけて極むる官位
notes.text: 'The office and rank you reach as your highest, according to your standing'. So a man from a lesser family who reaches the top of what his family can reach has the same right as a great noble at the top of his.
おほす is respectful: the 'someone' was a person of high rank. き: past that Kenkō experienced himself, so he heard it in person. Section 65 opens with the same frame.
